topic: IKEA flat-pack origin
angle: The flat-pack furniture format traces to a 1956 IKEA designer sawing the legs off a table to fit it in a car — turning shipping cost into the whole business model.

topic: How the Fed actually moves interest rates
angle: The Federal Reserve sets a target range for the federal funds rate and uses tools like interest on reserve balances to guide banks toward it — it does not 'print money' to do this.

topic: How credit card companies profit even when you pay in full
angle: Every card swipe generates an interchange fee paid by the merchant to the card issuer, so issuers earn revenue even from cardholders who never carry a balance.

topic: Blockbuster passed on buying Netflix
angle: In 2000 Netflix's founders offered to sell to Blockbuster for $50M and were turned down; Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010.

topic: What CPI actually measures
angle: The Consumer Price Index tracks price changes across a fixed basket of goods and services categories tracked by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, not a single price.

topic: How mortgage interest front-loads the early years
angle: Mortgage amortization schedules apply most of each early payment to interest and little to principal, gradually flipping over the life of the loan.

topic: Southwest's one-aircraft-type strategy
angle: Southwest Airlines flies only Boeing 737s across its whole fleet, cutting training, parts and maintenance costs versus mixed-fleet rivals.

topic: How fractional reserve banking works
angle: Banks are required to hold only a portion of deposits in reserve and can lend out the rest, which is how the banking system expands the money supply through lending.

topic: Netflix's DVD-to-streaming pivot
angle: Reed Hastings shifted Netflix from mailing DVDs to streaming starting 2007, cannibalizing its own core product before a competitor could.

topic: Why an inverted yield curve signals recession risk
angle: When short-term Treasury yields rise above long-term yields, it has historically preceded most US recessions, reflecting investor expectations of future rate cuts.

topic: Where the FICO credit score came from
angle: The Fair Isaac Corporation introduced the FICO score in 1989 to standardize lending risk assessment across US banks using a single three-digit number.

topic: Compound interest with a concrete example
angle: Compounding means interest earns interest on itself; the same principal and rate produce dramatically different totals depending purely on how many compounding periods elapse.

angle: Amazon ran on razor-thin retail margins for years while profits were funneled into building AWS, which became the real profit engine.

topic: How insurance companies actually profit
angle: Insurers price policies using actuarial tables that pool risk across many people, collecting more in premiums than they expect to pay out across the whole pool.

topic: McDonald's real estate business
angle: McDonald's Corporation owns much of the land under its restaurants and collects rent from franchisees, a model Ray Kroc's financier Harry Sonneborn engineered.

topic: What a stock split really changes
angle: A stock split multiplies the number of shares while dividing the price proportionally — the company's total market value and an investor's stake value don't change.

topic: Why store credit cards carry brutal interest rates
angle: Retail store credit cards often carry some of the highest APRs in the industry because they're underwritten for approval volume, not for the borrower's benefit.

topic: Gillette's razor-and-blades pricing
angle: Gillette popularized selling razors cheap (or at a loss) while pricing replacement blades high, a pricing pattern later copied by printers and razors alike.

topic: How short selling works and its unique risk
angle: Short sellers borrow and sell shares hoping to buy them back cheaper; because a stock's price has no ceiling, potential losses on a short are theoretically unlimited.

angle: Sears pioneered mail-order retail dominance in the early 1900s and filed for bankruptcy in 2018 after failing to adapt to e-commerce.

topic: What a bond actually is
angle: A bond is a loan an investor makes to a government or company, which pays periodic interest and returns principal at maturity.

topic: What a 401k match actually is
angle: An employer 401k match is additional compensation added only when an employee contributes, functioning as an immediate return on the employee's own contribution.

topic: Kodak invented and buried the digital camera
angle: A Kodak engineer built the first digital camera prototype in 1975; Kodak shelved it to protect its film business and later went bankrupt in 2012.

topic: Why index funds beat most active managers
angle: John Bogle launched the first retail index fund at Vanguard in 1976, betting that low-cost broad market tracking would beat costly active stock-picking over time.

topic: How payday loans trap borrowers

topic: Amazon's garage origin and Day 1 philosophy

angle: A buyback is a company repurchasing its own shares on the open market, reducing share count and (all else equal) raising earnings per remaining share.

angle: Every trade crosses a gap between the highest buy offer and lowest sell offer; that spread is a hidden cost paid on every buy-then-sell round trip.

angle: FDIC deposit insurance protects up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category — not an unlimited guarantee on everything in an account.

angle: The 1911 Supreme Court breakup of Standard Oil into 34 companies produced firms that evolved into ExxonMobil, Chevron and others.

topic: What a recession technically is
angle: In the US, recessions are officially dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research based on broad measures like employment and income, not just two negative GDP quarters.

angle: Banks process transactions in ways that can trigger multiple overdraft fees from a single low balance, turning a small shortfall into a recurring revenue source.

angle: When unpaid interest is added to a student loan's principal (capitalized), future interest is then charged on that larger balance, compounding the cost.

angle: Tesla built its own battery Gigafactory starting 2014 to control battery supply and cost instead of depending on outside cell makers.

topic: What quantitative easing actually does
angle: QE is a central bank buying large volumes of government bonds (and sometimes other assets) to push down long-term interest rates and add liquidity to the financial system.

topic: What a HELOC actually is
angle: A home equity line of credit lets a homeowner borrow repeatedly against home equity up to a limit, functioning more like a credit card secured by the house.

topic: Levi's 501 jeans origin
angle: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented copper-riveted work pants in 1873 for miners; the 501 design has stayed in production largely unchanged.

topic: How stock market circuit breakers work
angle: US exchanges pause trading automatically when the S&P 500 falls a set percentage in a session, giving the market a cooling-off period during panic selling.

topic: The limits of identity theft protection services
angle: Identity theft protection services monitor for misuse and help with recovery, but generally cannot prevent a breach or a determined identity thief from acting first.

topic: Why term life costs so much less than whole life
angle: Term life insurance only pays out if death occurs within a fixed period and builds no cash value, which is why it costs far less than permanent whole life coverage.

topic: Starbucks' site-selection science
angle: Starbucks uses detailed demographic and traffic-pattern analysis to choose store locations, historically clustering stores densely in target markets.

topic: What 'priced in' means
angle: Markets move on expectations, so a stock can drop on 'good' news if the results were already anticipated and priced into the share value beforehand.

topic: How check-cashing stores profit from the unbanked
angle: Check-cashing and prepaid-card services charge fees for basic transactions that a checking account would handle for free, disproportionately affecting unbanked consumers.

angle: LEGO nearly collapsed in 2003-2004 after over-diversifying into theme parks and clothing, then recovered by refocusing on its core brick sets.

topic: Dollar-cost averaging vs lump-sum investing
angle: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals smooths out purchase price over time, trading potential upside from lump-sum timing for reduced timing risk.

topic: What a credit freeze actually does
angle: A credit freeze restricts access to your credit report so new accounts generally can't be opened in your name, and by law it's free to place and lift.
